analysis.one_liner: Would have stopped a rule requiring retirement advisers to put savers' interests ahead of commissions.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 245-186 on October 27, 2015 — 242 of 246 Republicans for, 184 of 188 Democrats against — but the Senate never voted, and it did not become law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Labor Department from issuing its rule requiring people who advise 401(k) and IRA savers to act in the savers' best interest — a 'fiduciary' standard — until the Securities and Exchange Commission first issued its own rule for brokers. It also would have barred the SEC from issuing that rule until it first reported to Congress on whether the change would hurt brokers' commissions and their sales of their own investment products. The House passed it on a nearly straight party-line vote; the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and the bill died at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, broker-dealers and commission-based retirement advisers would have kept the current lower 'suitability' standard, which only requires that a recommendation fit a customer's situation, rather than a best-interest standard. Firms selling higher-fee mutual funds and annuities inside retirement accounts would have kept that revenue, and the SEC's path to any uniform standard would have been conditioned on first studying the impact on broker commissions, proprietary products, and the ability to sell from their own inventory.

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit the Labor Secretary from issuing any ERISA regulation defining who counts as a 'fiduciary' — someone legally bound to act in the client's best interest — until 60 days after the SEC issues a final conduct rule for brokers and dealers.

It would prohibit the SEC from issuing a rule applying an investment-adviser standard of conduct to brokers until it first reports to the House Financial Services and Senate Banking Committees on whether retail investors are actually harmed by the different standards, and on whether a uniform fiduciary standard would hurt brokers' commissions, their availability of proprietary products, and their ability to trade with customers from their own accounts.

It would require the SEC to publish formal Federal Register findings that any such rule would reduce customer confusion or harm, and to consider the differences in how brokers and advisers are registered, supervised, and examined.

analysis.who_pays: Retirement savers — ordinary workers with 401(k)s and IRAs — would have continued receiving advice under a standard that permits conflicted recommendations and commission-driven sales of higher-fee products, and would have waited on a slower, conditional path to any best-interest rule.

drawbacks.text: The bill layered new reporting and formal-findings requirements on any SEC fiduciary rule, and conditioned that rule on studies of its impact on broker commissions and proprietary products — a design that could delay a uniform best-interest standard for years, while retirement accounts kept paying commissions and fees on conflicted advice.

Supporters' strongest argument was real: brokers and investment advisers operate under different standards, which confuses retail customers, and the bill required the SEC to weigh cheaper disclosure and title fixes as alternatives; industry also argued a Labor Department-only rule could push advisers away from small accounts, reducing access to affordable advice. But the bill resolved that concern by delaying the stricter standard rather than by adopting any of the alternatives itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered procedural tidiness — one regulator, more studies, clearer titles — but its binding effect was to postpone the one standard that legally requires retirement advisers to put the saver's interest first, and to make even the SEC's version conditional on findings about brokers' commissions and proprietary-product sales. The costs fell on retirement savers; the benefits fell on firms earning those commissions. The SEC had already had the authority to set such a standard for five years without acting, so requiring the SEC to move first made the delay open-ended.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 245-186 but the Senate Banking Committee never scheduled it for a vote, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Ann Wagner introduced the bill on February 25, 2015, with 34 Republican cosponsors; it was referred to the Financial Services and Education and the Workforce Committees.

The Financial Services Committee ordered it reported 34-25 on September 30, 2015, and formally reported it on October 22, 2015 (H. Rept. 114-304), with the Education and the Workforce Committee discharged so the House could vote on the whole bill.
The Rules Committee structured the October 27 floor debate so the bill was closed to amendments, with only one Democratic amendment allowed a 10-minute debate.
The House passed it 245-186: 242 of 246 Republicans voted yes and 2 voted no, while only 3 of 188 Democrats voted yes and 184 voted no.
The Senate received the bill on October 28, 2015, and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broker-dealers and commission-based advisers kept the pre-existing rules, and Congress never enacted the bar it had passed. Retirement savers kept the possibility — realized shortly afterward when the Labor Department finalized its fiduciary rule — of a legal best-interest standard for advice on their retirement accounts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brokerage firms; the Labor Department bar never became law

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 242 of 246 Republicans voted yes while only 3 of 188 Democrats did, for a 245-186 final margin.

industries.note: The bill would have kept brokers on the lower 'suitability' standard and made any SEC best-interest rule conditional on first reporting to Congress about impacts on broker commissions, proprietary products, and principal trading — the very practices a fiduciary rule polices. Their gain came directly out of retirement savers' fees and commissions.

Annuities sold inside IRAs carry high commissions and were a main target of the Labor Department's fiduciary rule; delaying that rule would have preserved those sales. Savers would have kept paying the difference.

Advisers paid by product commissions would have kept the existing standard rather than a legal duty to act in the client's best interest; some argued the stricter rule would have pushed them away from serving small accounts.
